industry: Home security and alarm monitoring (incl. video doorbells, smart home)
words_and_claims_to_avoid: '80% of home robberies go unsolved' (GOLD-006): mislabels robbery vs burglary and lacks a source. Use FBI burglary clearance with year and source.
'Every home should have...' as an implied requirement; 'required by law/insurance' unless true.
'Free system' / 'free security system' without the monitoring contract, term, and fees right next to it (16 CFR 251).
'About $1 a day' unless that's the real all-in monthly price including required fees.
Implying police or government affiliation (badges, seals, 'official notice') or that a crime happened nearby unless true.
Claiming to be the customer's current provider, an 'upgrade', or that a competitor is going out of business (ADT v. Vivint pattern).
'Guaranteed protection' / 'burglar-proof' / 'police respond faster' without substantiation; insurance discount claims unless the insurer offers them.
compliance_notes: State alarm licensing: many states require the company license number in ads. California: alarm company operators must show name and BSIS license number in advertising (BPC 7599.44). Texas: name, address and license number in ads (Occ. Code 1702; 37 TAC 35.9). Client must confirm their state.
In-home sales of $25+: FTC Cooling-Off Rule 3-day cancellation notice (16 CFR 429). Many states add home-solicitation and door-to-door rules.
'Free equipment with monitoring': 16 CFR 251 - disclose the contract term, monthly fee, early termination fee, activation fees next to the offer.
Credit checks for financing: FCRA permissible purpose; FTC v. Vivint (2021) cost $20M for sales reps misusing credit reports.

Auto-renewal: the FTC 'click-to-cancel' rule was vacated by the 8th Circuit in July 2025, but state auto-renewal laws (e.g., CA BPC 17600 et seq.) still require clear renewal terms and easy cancellation.
Deceptive door-to-door impersonation of a competitor: Lanham Act / state UDAP exposure (ADT v. Vivint $10M settlement, 2018).
Statistics: cite source and year; 'robbery' and 'burglary' are different crimes in FBI data.
TCPA applies to follow-up calls/texts from QR or call-me forms; get consent.
standing_rules: Emotion-agnostic: fear, joy, pride, status, relief, nostalgia are all options; the client chooses.
Every angle and combo carries a sell-the-outcome line.
Unverified (agency/vendor-only) results are labeled; never quote them as fact on a card.
No age/demographic angle unless a cited source supports it for this industry; even then, check Fair Housing / ECOA before using it in housing or credit.

emotion_by_offer.why: Upfront cost is a barrier; 'free install / $0 activation' (GOLD-001, 002, 004) removes it while the monthly contract is the real price. Works when paired with a clear threat-to-safety story.
emotion_by_offer.reinforcing_photo: Tech installing a keypad / doorbell cam at a real front door.
emotion_by_offer.what_backfires: Hiding contract length/fees (FTC 'free' rules); masked-burglar clip art (GOLD-005) looks cheap.

emotion_by_offer_conflicts.conflict: GOLD-006 '80% of home robberies go unsolved' vs FBI data
emotion_by_offer_conflicts.resolution: Law/accuracy wins: robbery and burglary differ; use 'about 86% of burglaries were not cleared (FBI, 2019)' with source line, or a newer FBI figure.

emotion_by_offer_conflicts.conflict: Blevins 2012 burglar stats vs funding source
emotion_by_offer_conflicts.resolution: Usable but label 'industry-funded survey' internally; on cards cite as 'UNC Charlotte study' with year, no exaggeration (e.g., 'about 6 in 10 said an alarm would make them move on').

emotion_by_offer_conflicts.conflict: Gold 'free system' cards (GOLD-001, 004) vs FTC Free Guide
emotion_by_offer_conflicts.resolution: Law wins: keep 'free' only with term, fee and ETF disclosed next to the offer.

emotion_by_offer_conflicts.conflict: Fear-led gold samples (GOLD-005 masked burglar) vs C-3PO craft rubric
emotion_by_offer_conflicts.resolution: Emotion stays allowed (Patrick's rule); the craft fix is a real night-house scene instead of clip art.
